items.title: An Architect on Designing Homes
items.tvi: Kiến trúc sư bàn về thiết kế nhà
lines: You've said that most new apartments are designed for people who don't exist. What do you mean by that?

Developers tend to design for an imaginary average family: two parents, two children, both adults working nine to five. But that family is becoming the exception. We have elderly people living alone, adult children living with parents well into their thirties, people working from home. The standard layout simply doesn't fit.
So what would you do differently?

Flexibility, above all. Walls that can be moved without major building work, rooms that can be divided or combined as needs change. In one project, we designed apartments where a small studio could be separated from the main flat with its own entrance, so a grandparent could live independently but close by.
Isn't that more expensive to build?

Initially, slightly. But if you consider that people won't need to move every time their life changes, it's far more economical over the lifetime of the building. The real obstacle isn't cost, it's habit. Developers know what sells, and they're reluctant to take risks.
Are you optimistic that this will change?
Cautiously. Buyers are becoming more demanding, and once a few developers prove the model works, others usually follow.

qs.q: What is the architect's criticism of most new apartments?
qs.a: They are designed for a family type that is increasingly rare
w: They are too small for families
They are too expensive for young people

qs.q: Why does he believe flexible design is economical in the long term?
qs.a: People won't need to move when their situation changes

qs.q: What does he see as the main obstacle?
qs.a: Developers' unwillingness to change habits

items.title: A Lecture on Misinformation
items.tvi: Bài giảng về tin sai lệch
items.text: One of the most counterintuitive findings in research on misinformation is that correcting a false claim can sometimes make people remember it more strongly. If a news story repeats a myth in order to debunk it, some readers later recall the myth but forget that it was false. Repetition, it seems, breeds familiarity, and familiarity is easily mistaken for truth. This doesn't mean we should stop correcting falsehoods; on balance, corrections do reduce belief in misinformation. But it does suggest that how we correct matters enormously. Researchers now recommend leading with the facts rather than the myth, mentioning the false claim only once, and explaining why it is wrong, not merely that it is wrong. People find it difficult to abandon an explanation unless they are offered a better one to replace it. Another promising approach is so-called prebunking: warning people in advance about the techniques used to mislead them, such as emotional language or fake experts. Rather like a vaccine, this seems to give people a degree of resistance before they encounter the misinformation itself.

qs.q: What is surprising about correcting false claims?
qs.a: Repeating a myth can make people remember it

qs.q: Why should corrections explain why a claim is wrong?
qs.a: People need a better explanation to replace the false one

qs.q: How is 'prebunking' compared to a vaccine?
qs.a: It gives resistance before exposure to misinformation
w: It must be repeated every year

items.title: Two Colleagues on Remote Meetings
items.tvi: Hai đồng nghiệp bàn về họp trực tuyến
lines: Did you find this morning's video call as exhausting as I did?
Completely. Three hours of staring at faces in little boxes. I felt as if I'd run a marathon.
I read somewhere that it's because you can't pick up on body language properly, so your brain works harder to read people.
That makes sense. And there's the awkwardness of not knowing when to speak. In a room, you'd see someone take a breath before talking. Online, everyone interrupts each other and then apologises.
I've started suggesting we turn cameras off for part of the meeting, especially when someone's just presenting slides.
Hasn't the boss objected? She likes to see that people are paying attention.
She was reluctant at first, but I pointed out that half the team were looking at their own image anyway, which is hardly paying attention.
Ha, fair point. Personally, I think most of these meetings could be an email.

qs.q: According to the woman, why are video calls tiring?
qs.a: It is harder to read body language

qs.q: What argument did she use to persuade the boss?
qs.a: Many people were watching themselves rather than the meeting
w: Cameras use too much internet data
The boss can't see everyone anyway

qs.q: What does the man suggest at the end?
qs.a: Many meetings are unnecessary
w: Everyone should return to the office

items.title: A Radio Piece on Urban Heat
items.tvi: Phóng sự về nhiệt đô thị
items.text: On a summer afternoon, the centre of a large city can be several degrees hotter than the countryside just a few kilometres away. This is known as the urban heat island effect, and it's caused by the materials cities are built from. Concrete, asphalt and dark rooftops absorb heat during the day and release it slowly at night, so temperatures never fall as much as they should. Air conditioners make the problem worse, pumping hot air into the streets to keep buildings cool. The consequences are far from trivial. Heat waves are now one of the deadliest forms of extreme weather, particularly for elderly people and outdoor workers. Fortunately, the solutions are relatively well understood. Planting trees can reduce street temperatures significantly, while painting roofs white reflects sunlight rather than absorbing it. Some cities are going further, building so-called green corridors, linked parks and waterways that allow cooler air to flow through dense neighbourhoods. The challenge is less technical than financial: such measures require long-term investment, and their benefits, while substantial, are spread across many years.

qs.q: What causes the urban heat island effect?
qs.a: Building materials that store and release heat

qs.q: How do air conditioners affect the problem?
qs.a: They make streets hotter

qs.q: What is the main challenge, according to the speaker?
qs.a: Funding long-term projects

items.title: Interview with a Translator
lines: You've translated more than thirty novels from Vietnamese into English. What's the hardest part?

Without doubt, forms of address. Vietnamese uses kinship terms constantly: anh, chị, em, cô, chú. Each one tells you about age, relationship, even emotional distance. English has just 'you'. A whole layer of meaning disappears unless you find other ways to express it.
How do you deal with that?

It depends. Sometimes I convey it through tone, or through what characters call each other in narration. Occasionally I leave the Vietnamese term in place, if it's been explained earlier. But I try not to do that too often, because it can make the text feel exotic in a way the original never was.
Do authors ever object to your choices?

Some like to be closely involved, others prefer not to read the translation at all. One author told me, 'Once it's in English, it's your book as much as mine.' I found that generous, but also a little frightening.
Because it reminds you how much responsibility you carry. Readers in English will judge the author by my words.

qs.q: Why are Vietnamese forms of address difficult to translate?
qs.a: They carry information that English 'you' does not

qs.q: Why does the translator avoid keeping Vietnamese terms too often?
qs.a: It can make the text seem strange in a way the original was not

qs.q: Why did the author's comment feel frightening?
qs.a: It showed how responsible the translator is
w: The author refused to read it

items.title: A Talk on Decision Fatigue
items.tvi: Bài nói về mệt mỏi khi ra quyết định
items.text: Have you ever noticed that you make worse choices at the end of a long day? Psychologists call this decision fatigue: the idea that our capacity to make careful decisions gets used up, rather like a muscle that tires with use. One frequently quoted study of judges found that they were far more likely to grant prisoners parole early in the morning and just after lunch, and far less likely to do so just before a break. When tired, the researchers suggested, people tend to fall back on the default option, which for a judge is to say no. I should add that this study has been criticised, and some of its findings may have other explanations. But the general idea fits many people's experience, and it has practical implications. Some successful people deliberately reduce trivial decisions, wearing similar clothes every day or eating the same breakfast, so that they have more energy for decisions that matter. You don't need to go that far, but it may be worth scheduling important choices for the morning, and being a little suspicious of anything you decide at eleven o'clock at night.

qs.q: What did the study of judges suggest?
qs.a: Tired judges tended to choose the safer default
w: Judges worked better in the evening
Judges made more decisions after lunch

qs.q: What does the speaker say about the study?
qs.a: It has been criticised by other researchers

qs.q: What practical advice does the speaker give?
qs.a: Make important decisions earlier in the day
w: Wear the same clothes every day

items.title: Discussing a Business Proposal
items.tvi: Bàn về một đề xuất kinh doanh
lines: I've read your proposal for the subscription service. The idea's strong, but I'm not convinced by the figures.
You're assuming that thirty percent of trial users will become paying customers. Industry averages are closer to ten or fifteen.
That's true for most services, but our pilot in Da Nang converted twenty-eight percent.
That's encouraging, but it's a small sample, and they were mostly people who already knew the brand. I'd want to see the model work at fifteen percent before we invest.
If we plan for fifteen, we'd need to cut marketing costs by about a third.
Then let's look at that. If the business only works with optimistic numbers, it's not a business, it's a hope.
Fair enough. I'll revise the projections and send you two versions, one conservative and one based on the pilot.

qs.q: What is the woman's main concern?
qs.a: The expected number of paying customers is too high

qs.q: Why is she not convinced by the pilot results?
qs.a: The group was small and already knew the brand
w: The pilot took place in the wrong city

qs.q: What will the man do next?
qs.a: Prepare two sets of figures
w: Run another pilot in Da Nang

items.title: A Museum Curator's Talk
items.tvi: Bài nói của người phụ trách bảo tàng
items.text: When visitors come to this exhibition, they often ask why some of the objects look so ordinary: a broken bowl, a child's sandal, a handful of coins. They expect a museum to be full of treasures. But for archaeologists, everyday objects are often far more revealing than gold. A king's crown tells us about one person; a cooking pot tells us about thousands. From the residue left inside these pots, for instance, we've been able to work out what people ate, which crops they grew and even how trade routes connected this coast to China and India. The sandal you see in the third case belonged to a child of perhaps six or seven. We know that because of its size, but also because it was repaired three times, suggesting the family couldn't afford a new one. Small details like that bring the past to life in a way that treasure rarely does. So as you walk around today, I'd encourage you to spend as much time with the humble objects as with the spectacular ones.

qs.q: Why are everyday objects valuable to archaeologists?
qs.a: They reveal how ordinary people lived

qs.q: What have researchers learned from the cooking pots?
qs.a: Details about diet and trade
w: The names of the people who used them

qs.q: What does the repaired sandal suggest?
qs.a: The family had little money
w: Sandals were rare at that time

items.title: Friends Discuss Volunteering Abroad
items.tvi: Bạn bè bàn về tình nguyện ở nước ngoài
lines: I'm thinking of doing one of those volunteer programmes abroad next summer. Teaching English in a village school.
Have you looked into it properly? Some of those programmes have a terrible reputation.

Well, some charge volunteers thousands of dollars, and very little of that money reaches the community. And a lot of them send unqualified people to teach for just two weeks, which can actually be more disruptive than helpful for the children.
I hadn't thought about that. So should I not go at all?
I'm not saying that. Just choose carefully. Look for programmes that are run by local organisations, that ask for a longer commitment, and that are transparent about where the money goes.
That makes sense. Maybe I could do something closer to home, too. There's a literacy project in our own city.
Exactly. Sometimes the most useful thing isn't the most exotic one.

qs.q: What problem with some programmes does the man mention?
qs.a: Short stays by unqualified volunteers can harm children's learning
w: Volunteers are not allowed to teach

qs.q: What kind of programme does he recommend?
qs.a: One run locally and open about its finances

qs.q: What does the man suggest in his final comment?
qs.a: Helpful work does not need to be far away

items.title: A Report on Food Waste
items.tvi: Phóng sự về lãng phí thực phẩm
items.text: Roughly a third of all food produced worldwide is never eaten. In poorer countries, most of this loss happens early in the supply chain, through inadequate storage, transport and refrigeration. In wealthier countries, by contrast, the largest share is thrown away by shops and households. Supermarkets reject fruit and vegetables that are the wrong shape or size, and consumers routinely discard food that is perfectly safe simply because it has passed a 'best before' date. Many people confuse this with a 'use by' date, which genuinely relates to safety. 'Best before' is merely about quality: a biscuit may be slightly less crisp, but it's not going to make you ill. Some countries are now taking action. France has made it illegal for large supermarkets to throw away unsold food that is still edible; it must instead be donated to charities. Elsewhere, apps connect restaurants with customers who can buy leftover meals cheaply at the end of the day. Such measures help, but campaigners argue that real change will require a shift in attitudes, so that we see food not as something disposable but as something that took resources, energy and labour to produce.

qs.q: Where is most food lost in poorer countries?
qs.a: Early in the supply chain

qs.q: What is the difference between 'best before' and 'use by'?
qs.a: 'Best before' is about quality, 'use by' about safety

qs.q: What does French law require?
qs.a: Large supermarkets must donate edible unsold food
w: Shops must sell food more cheaply

items.title: A Debate about Homework
items.tvi: Tranh luận về bài tập về nhà
lines: Your school has recently abolished homework for students under fourteen. Why?

We looked closely at the research, and for younger students the evidence that homework improves learning is surprisingly weak. What we did find was that it caused a great deal of conflict at home and that it widened the gap between children whose parents could help them and those whose parents couldn't.
But surely practice matters. How else do children consolidate what they learn?

Practice does matter, but it doesn't have to happen at the kitchen table at nine in the evening. We've extended the school day slightly so that students do supervised practice with teachers available. Reading at home is still encouraged, but it isn't compulsory or marked.
Some parents have complained that they no longer know what their children are learning.

That's a fair point, and frankly it's something we underestimated. We're now sending a short weekly summary to families. Homework was never a very good way of keeping parents informed anyway, but we hadn't replaced that function.

qs.q: According to the head teacher, what did homework do for younger students?
qs.a: It increased inequality between families
w: It helped parents understand the curriculum

qs.q: How does the school now provide practice?
qs.a: Through supervised sessions during a longer school day

qs.q: How does the head teacher respond to the parents' complaint?
qs.a: She admits it is a valid criticism
w: She says the parents are wrong
She says nothing can be done

qs.q: What does she imply about homework's role in informing parents?
qs.a: It did this badly, but the school still needed to replace it
w: It was the best way to inform parents

items.title: A Lecture on Sleep and Memory
items.tvi: Bài giảng về giấc ngủ và trí nhớ
items.text: Today I want to look at the relationship between sleep and memory, which is one of the more robust findings in recent psychology. For a long time, sleep was thought of as a passive state, a kind of switching off. We now know that the sleeping brain is extremely active, and that one of the things it appears to be doing is reorganising information acquired during the day. In a typical experiment, participants learn a list of word pairs in the evening and are tested the next morning. Those who sleep between learning and testing generally remember significantly more than those who stay awake for the same period. What is particularly interesting is that sleep doesn't just protect memories; it seems to help us extract patterns from them. In some studies, people who slept were more likely to notice a hidden rule in a set of problems than those who didn't. Now, I should add a note of caution. Many of these studies involve small groups of young university students, and we don't yet know how well the findings apply to older adults or to more complex, real-world learning. But the practical message for you as students is fairly clear: staying up all night before an exam is likely to be counterproductive.

qs.q: How was sleep traditionally viewed, according to the lecturer?
qs.a: As a state in which the brain was inactive
w: As the most important part of learning
As a cause of memory loss

qs.q: What did participants who slept do better in the experiment?
qs.a: They remembered more word pairs
w: They learned the pairs faster in the evening
They made fewer mistakes when tired

qs.q: What additional benefit of sleep does the lecturer describe?
qs.a: It may help people identify patterns

qs.q: Why does the lecturer add “a note of caution”?
qs.a: The research may not apply to all groups of people
w: Some studies were found to be dishonest
Sleep can damage memory in older adults

items.title: Two Friends Discuss a Job Offer
items.tvi: Hai người bạn bàn về lời mời làm việc
lines: So, have you decided about the job in Singapore?
Not yet. On paper it's an obvious yes. The salary's almost double, the company's highly respected and it would look great on my CV.
But I've only just settled here. I've finally got a group of friends, I've started volunteering at weekends, and my parents are getting older. I'd be four hours away by plane.
Four hours isn't the end of the world. Lots of people manage it.
I know. And part of me thinks I'll regret it forever if I turn it down. It's the kind of opportunity that doesn't come twice.
Can you negotiate? Ask to start later, or to work from here part of the time?
I could try. They said they're flexible about the start date. I hadn't thought of asking for anything more than that.
Well, you've got nothing to lose by asking. The worst they can say is no.

qs.q: What attracts the woman to the job?
qs.a: The pay and the company's reputation
w: The chance to live near her parents

qs.q: Why is she hesitant?
qs.a: She has recently built a life where she is
w: She doubts her ability to do the job

qs.q: What is the man's attitude to the distance?
qs.a: He thinks it is manageable
w: He thinks it is a serious problem
He has not thought about it

qs.q: What does the man encourage her to do?
qs.a: Ask the company for better conditions

items.title: A Podcast on Tourism in Small Towns
items.tvi: Podcast về du lịch ở thị trấn nhỏ
items.text: When a small town suddenly becomes popular with tourists, the effects can be dramatic. I visited a mountain village last year that had appeared in a popular film, and within two years, visitor numbers had risen from a few thousand to nearly half a million. On the positive side, families who used to struggle to make a living from farming now run guesthouses and cafés, and young people who had left for the cities have started to return. But the residents I spoke to were far from unanimously happy. Rents have risen so sharply that some long-term residents can no longer afford to live in the centre. Traditional shops have been replaced by souvenir stalls, and the narrow streets are often so crowded that older people avoid going out at weekends. One woman told me, rather sadly, that she now feels like an extra in someone else's photograph. The local council has started to respond, limiting the number of tour buses and introducing a small visitor fee to fund public services. Whether these measures will be enough is still unclear, but at least the village is asking the right question: not how to attract more tourists, but how to benefit from them without losing itself.

qs.q: What caused the sudden rise in visitors?
qs.a: The village appeared in a film
w: A new airport was built nearby
The village won a tourism award

qs.q: Which positive effect does the speaker mention?
qs.a: Young people have moved back to the village

qs.q: What does the woman's comment about photographs suggest?
qs.a: She feels her home has become a tourist attraction rather than a community
w: She enjoys being photographed by visitors
She has started a photography business

qs.q: What is the speaker's view of the council's measures?
qs.a: They are a sensible start, though their success is uncertain
w: They will certainly solve the problem
They are likely to make things worse

items.title: Feedback on a Research Proposal
items.tvi: Góp ý cho đề cương nghiên cứu
lines: Thanks for sending your proposal. I've read it carefully, and I think the topic is genuinely interesting.
Thank you. I was worried it was too broad.
Well, that's my main concern, actually. You want to study how social media affects the mental health of teenagers in three different countries. That's at least three projects, not one.
I see. So should I choose one country?

I'd go further than that. Focus on one specific question you can actually answer in eighteen months. For example, whether time spent on one particular platform is related to sleep quality among sixteen-year-olds in one city.
It is narrow, and that's a strength. A small question answered well is far more useful than a big question answered vaguely. You can always widen the scope later.
All right. I'll rewrite the research question and send you a new version next week.

qs.q: What is the supervisor's main concern about the proposal?
qs.a: It is too wide in scope

qs.q: What does the supervisor recommend?
qs.a: Focusing on a single, specific question

qs.q: How does the student first react to the suggested example?
qs.a: She thinks it may be too limited
w: She says it has already been studied

qs.q: What is the supervisor's attitude to narrow research questions?
qs.a: They can be an advantage
